title: Slide Insurance's Third-Quarter Profit Rises 24.5% to $138 Million on a 59.3% Combined Ratio, With a $1.50 Special Dividend and a Raised Net Income Outlook
summary: Florida homeowners insurer Slide Insurance reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $138.2 million, up 24.5%, on a 59.3% combined ratio, declared a $1.50 one-time special dividend and raised its 2026 net income outlook to $500 million to $520 million, while flagging up to $50 million of pre-tax Hurricane Isaias losses in the fourth quarter.
description:
Slide Insurance Holdings, a Florida-based homeowners insurer listed on Nasdaq under the symbol SLDE, reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 27, 2026, for the quarter ended September 30. The release shows a company that is growing quickly and earning very high margins on paper, while telling investors that a hurricane that arrived after the quarter ended will cost it money in the fourth. For anyone trying to judge the health of the Florida property market, the report is a useful data point because it comes from a carrier whose business is concentrated in the state.

Net income for the quarter was $138.2 million, up 24.5 per cent from $111.0 million in the third quarter of 2025. Diluted earnings per share were $1.09 against $0.79, an increase of 37.3 per cent, helped by a smaller share count: weighted average diluted shares fell to 127.1 million from 140.1 million. Pre-tax income was $161.7 million, up from $147.0 million, and income tax expense fell to $23.5 million from $36.0 million, which explains why net income grew faster than pre-tax income. Total revenue rose 35.9 per cent to $361.1 million.

Premium growth was strong. Gross premiums written, the premium before reinsurance, were $506.6 million, up 9.3 per cent from $463.4 million. The company attributes growth to voluntary new business, renewals of policies it previously acquired from Citizens Property Insurance, Florida's state-backed insurer of last resort, and launches in new states. Net premiums earned, the portion of premium recognised as revenue after reinsurance, rose 37.1 per cent to $333.3 million. The gap between the two growth rates reflects the timing of premium recognition: written premium is booked when policies are issued, while earned premium follows over the life of the policy, so a book that has grown quickly shows earned premium catching up.

The combined ratio, which adds the loss ratio and the expense ratio and indicates underwriting profit when it is below 100 per cent, was 59.3 per cent, up from 48.5 per cent a year earlier. The loss ratio was 30.4 per cent against 13.7 per cent, and the expense ratio was 28.9 per cent against 34.8 per cent. The company says the deterioration in the combined ratio came mainly from catastrophe losses, which were benign in the prior-year period. This quarter included $34.2 million of Florida convective storm losses, partly offset by $18.0 million of favorable development on prior-period reserves. Excluding catastrophes and prior-period development, the accident year loss ratio, a non-GAAP measure, improved to 25.5 per cent from 27.5 per cent. For the nine months, the combined ratio was 57.4 per cent against 58.3 per cent, and net income was $412.6 million against $273.6 million.

Readers should interpret such a low combined ratio with care. The figure reflects what the company retains after buying reinsurance, and ceded premiums earned were $146.0 million in the quarter, up from $116.3 million, and $386.5 million for the nine months, up from $296.0 million. The release does not describe the structure, retentions or limits of the reinsurance programme, so it is not possible from this document to say how much of the underwriting profit comes from the cost of reinsurance versus the quality of the underlying risks. Balance sheet data show the scale of the programme: prepaid reinsurance premiums were $397.8 million at September 30, up from $202.7 million at the end of 2025, and reinsurance premiums payable were $324.2 million.

Return on equity for the quarter was 11.1 per cent, against 12.1 per cent, which the company says annualises to 44.4 per cent. For the nine months, return on equity was 34.2 per cent against 39.2 per cent. Those numbers are very high by industry standards, and the company expects a full-year return above 40 per cent. Shareholders' equity was $1.30 billion at quarter end, up from $1.11 billion at year-end 2025, and total assets were $3.39 billion.

Capital return is a large part of the story. The board declared a regular quarterly dividend of $0.07 per share and a one-time special dividend of $1.50 per share, both payable on November 30, 2026, to holders of record on November 23. The company estimates it has returned $423.1 million since its June 2025 initial public offering, made up of $192.2 million of dividends and $230.9 million of share repurchases. It made no repurchases in the third quarter and has $114.1 million remaining under its programme. Separately, the company entered a new credit agreement on October 27 with a syndicate led by Huntington National Bank. It totals $1.07 billion, replaces an existing $530.4 million agreement and is to be used for general corporate purposes, including refinancing debt and supporting growth.

The outlook was raised. Slide now expects 2026 net income of $500 million to $520 million, up from $455 million to $470 million, and gross premiums written of $1.90 billion to $1.95 billion, with the low end raised from $1.85 billion. The outlook includes up to $50 million of pre-tax losses from Hurricane Isaias in the fourth quarter. The release gives no further detail on that event. Other reports in this series have noted that Isaias made landfall in the Florida Panhandle after the end of the third quarter and that modelers' estimates of industry losses vary widely, so the fourth-quarter number is the one to watch.

Growth beyond Florida is part of the plan. Management says it expects double-digit growth outside Florida and selective growth inside the state that meets its return threshold. It is building a residential excess and surplus lines business in California, expanding homeowners cover in South Carolina and Rhode Island, and began writing residential business in Texas in October 2026. Chief executive Bruce Lucas described the quarter as another period of strong results and disciplined execution and cited a book of business of nearly $2 billion.

What should readers take from this? First, the third quarter was an unusually quiet one for Florida catastrophe losses for this company, and the margin is exceptional because of that. Second, the company's own guidance shows that it expects a hurricane loss in the fourth quarter, so a full-year view is more informative than any single quarter. Third, the amount of capital being returned, and a larger credit facility, suggest management is confident about the balance sheet, although that confidence has yet to be tested by a large storm. The company's conference call on October 28 may add detail on reinsurance and the cost of Isaias.
image_alt: Residential houses representing Florida homeowners insurance (illustrative)
key_points: Third-quarter net income was $138.2 million, up 24.5% from $111.0 million, and diluted earnings per share were $1.09 against $0.79 a year earlier.
The combined ratio was 59.3% against 48.5%, with $34.2 million of Florida convective storm losses and $18.0 million of favorable prior-period development; the nine-month ratio was 57.4%.
Gross premiums written rose 9.3% to $506.6 million and net premiums earned rose 37.1% to $333.3 million, while ceded premiums earned increased to $146.0 million from $116.3 million.

The board declared a $0.07 quarterly dividend and a one-time $1.50 special dividend, both payable November 30, 2026, and a new $1.07 billion credit facility led by Huntington National Bank replaces a $530.4 million agreement.

The company raised its 2026 net income outlook to $500 million to $520 million from $455 million to $470 million and guided to gross premiums written of $1.90 billion to $1.95 billion, including up to $50 million of pre-tax Hurricane Isaias losses in the fourth quarter.
why_it_matters: Slide is one of the new Florida-focused homeowners carriers built from policies taken out of the state's Citizens insurer, so its results are a read on whether private capital can profit from Florida property risk. A quarter with very low catastrophe losses flatters the numbers, and the company itself flags a hurricane loss still to come in the fourth quarter.

title: Universal Insurance Holdings' Third-Quarter Net Income Rises 32% to $52.5 Million as the Combined Ratio Falls to 91.0% and Florida Premiums Slip 3.3%
summary: Universal Insurance Holdings reported third-quarter 2026 net income available to common of $52.5 million, up 31.8%, with a 91.0% net combined ratio, 32.7% annualized return on common equity and 7.9% growth in policies in force, while Florida direct premiums written fell 3.3% and other states grew 18.5%.
description:
Universal Insurance Holdings, a Florida homeowners insurer, published its third-quarter 2026 results on October 22, 2026, in a Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The figures show a company that is earning more on each dollar of premium, growing policy counts outside its home state and spending less on reinsurance than a year ago. They also show a business that remains heavily dependent on Florida, where premium written declined during the quarter.

The headline numbers are as follows. Net income available to common shareholders was $52.5 million, up 31.8 per cent from $39.8 million in the third quarter of 2025. Diluted earnings per share were $1.80 compared with $1.38, an increase of 30.4 per cent. Operating income rose 32.8 per cent to $72.2 million, an operating margin of 16.4 per cent, and a non-GAAP adjusted operating income measure rose 44.5 per cent to $77.2 million. Adjusted diluted earnings per share were $1.93 against $1.36. Annualised return on common equity was 32.7 per cent, slightly below 33.4 per cent a year earlier, and book value per share was $23.37, up 32.4 per cent from $17.65. Chief executive Stephen Donaghy said the company delivered a very strong return on equity driven by solid underwriting and revenue performance.

Underwriting improved. The net combined ratio, which adds the loss ratio and expense ratio after reinsurance, fell to 91.0 per cent from 96.4 per cent. The net loss ratio was 64.6 per cent compared with 70.2 per cent, and the net expense ratio was 26.4 per cent against 26.2 per cent, with the policy acquisition cost ratio unchanged at 17.7 per cent and the other operating cost ratio at 8.7 per cent. Losses and loss adjustment expenses were $260.5 million compared with $252.3 million, so the improvement came because earned premium grew faster than losses, with net premiums earned rising 12.1 per cent to $403.2 million. Over nine months, the net combined ratio was 90.8 per cent against 96.4 per cent, and net income available to common was $166.0 million, up 42.7 per cent.

Premium trends are more mixed. Direct premiums written rose 2.7 per cent to $608.9 million. Florida premiums fell 3.3 per cent to $414.4 million, while premiums in other states grew 18.5 per cent to $194.5 million. That means roughly a third of direct premium written now comes from outside Florida. Policies in force rose 7.9 per cent to 953,611, of which 598,104 were in Florida, up from 561,546, and 355,507 were in other states, up from 322,342. Premiums in force grew 4.4 per cent to $2.23 billion. Total insured value, the sum of property values the company insures, reached $429.6 billion, up from $385.0 billion, with $198.4 billion in Florida and $231.2 billion elsewhere. Donaghy said new business trends were solid, including 8 per cent growth in policies in force.

The explanation for falling Florida premium alongside rising policy counts is not given in the release, which means the reader should avoid assuming a cause. Falling premium per policy in a state can result from rate decreases, changes in coverage choices or mix, and other factors. The release does not break these down. What it does show is that average premium in force per Florida policy is about $2,621, from $2,800 a year earlier, which is simple arithmetic from the premiums in force and policy counts in the table and not a figure reported by the company.

Reinsurance changed. The company's new reinsurance programme incepted on June 1, 2026. The ceded premium ratio, the share of premium handed to reinsurers, fell to 27.6 per cent in the quarter from 32.7 per cent, and to 30.3 per cent for the nine months from 31.5 per cent. Ceded premiums earned in the quarter were $153.5 million against $174.4 million, a decline of 12.0 per cent. The company links the new programme to lower commission revenue, since commissions it received on ceded premium fell, and commissions, policy fees and other revenue declined 10.8 per cent to $19.6 million. On the balance sheet, prepaid reinsurance premiums rose to $409.3 million, and reinsurance recoverables fell to $157.0 million from $232.9 million, reflecting recoveries collected from earlier losses.

Hurricane Isaias is the main uncertainty. The release states that the storm made landfall near Destin, in the western Florida Panhandle, as a Category 2 hurricane after the end of the quarter and weakened quickly inland. The claims team deployed field adjusters and worked to speed inspections and payments. Donaghy said claims activity to date had been less significant than initially anticipated. The release does not give a loss estimate or a reserve impact, so the cost to Universal is not known from this document. Earlier articles on this site discussed the wide range of modeler estimates for industry losses, and a company that writes mostly in Florida will be sensitive to where the storm's wind and rain fell.

Capital management was modest. The company repurchased about 174 thousand shares for about $7.4 million in the quarter, with about $1.1 million left under its authorisation, and declared a quarterly dividend of $0.16 per share, bringing dividends declared to $0.48 per share for the nine months. Stockholders' equity was $646.0 million at September 30 against $551.0 million at year-end 2025, and debt was $97.3 million. The company provided no financial guidance for 2026 or later periods.

For readers, the main points are straightforward. The company's underwriting results are improving, in step with other Florida carriers. Growth is increasingly coming from outside Florida, which diversifies the book but also exposes the company to other hazards. And the full effect of Isaias, together with the reinsurance cost and recoverable position that follows, will be visible in the fourth-quarter results rather than in this report.
image_alt: Coastal houses representing Florida property insurance (illustrative)
key_points: Net income available to common was $52.5 million, up 31.8%, and diluted earnings per share were $1.80 against $1.38 a year earlier.
The net combined ratio improved to 91.0% from 96.4%, with the net loss ratio at 64.6% against 70.2% and the net expense ratio at 26.4%.
Direct premiums written rose 2.7% to $608.9 million, but Florida premiums fell 3.3% to $414.4 million while other states grew 18.5% to $194.5 million.
Policies in force grew 7.9% to 953,611 and total insured value reached $429.6 billion, with 355,507 policies now outside Florida.

A new reinsurance programme incepted June 1, 2026 cut the ceded premium ratio to 27.6% in the quarter, and Hurricane Isaias, which struck after the quarter ended, had produced claims activity 'less significant than initially anticipated' with no loss estimate given.
why_it_matters: Universal is a major private Florida homeowners insurer, so its figures show how the market is moving toward profit after years of losses. The shift of growth to other states and lower reinsurance spending are the changes to watch, along with the cost of Hurricane Isaias, which the company has not yet quantified.

title: UAE's New Takaful Regulation Took Effect on September 14: Separate Legal Funds, a Mandatory Wakala Model and Strict Rules for Islamic Windows at Conventional Insurers
summary: The Central Bank of the UAE replaced its 2022 takaful rules with a regulation effective September 14, 2026 that requires each operator to run a legally separate takaful fund, use a wakala-based model at all times and, for conventional insurers with Islamic windows, obtain approval and keep separate accounts and sharia governance.
description:
The Central Bank of the UAE has replaced its rulebook for takaful, or Islamic insurance, with a new regulation that took effect on September 14, 2026. The change was reported by the law firm Pinsent Masons on September 29, by Emirates 24|7 on September 30 and discussed earlier by the Dubai law firm Al Tamimi & Company on August 11. Together, the sources describe a regime that tightens how takaful money is separated and governed, while at the same time allowing conventional insurers to enter the market through Islamic windows.

First, some background on how takaful differs from conventional insurance. In a takaful arrangement, participants contribute money to a common fund that pays claims for members who suffer a loss, and an operator manages the fund for a fee. The central legal and sharia questions concern who owns the fund, how the operator is paid, and whether a deficit or surplus belongs to participants or to the company. Regulators therefore tend to focus on how the fund is separated from the operator's own balance sheet. The new UAE regulation, called the Regulation regarding takaful insurance, addresses this directly.

The most significant requirement is a dedicated takaful insurance fund. Pinsent Masons reports that every licensed takaful operator must establish a fund with its own legal personality and separate financial liability, and the fund's assets and liabilities must be fully segregated from those of the company. Policy obligations are met from the assets of the fund, but claims remain enforceable against the company, which stays responsible for settling them properly and on time. Al Tamimi, writing about the underlying standards, adds that the fund must be independent of the company and registered with the Central Bank, that its charter requires approval from the board, the internal sharia supervision committee, the Central Bank and the Higher Shari'ah Authority, and that it must own its assets, bear its liabilities and show an independent financial position in the company's accounts. The firm also reports that the fund has a renewable term of 100 years and that a company with more than one takaful line must run a separate fund for each.

The second requirement concerns the operating model. According to Pinsent Masons, operators must use a wakala-based model at all times. Wakala is an agency structure in which the operator manages the fund on behalf of participants in return for a fee. Under the 2022 rules, wakala could be combined with mudaraba, a profit-sharing arrangement, or another model approved by the Central Bank and the Higher Shari'ah Authority. Firms that currently use a mudaraba element may therefore need to restructure. Al Tamimi notes that the operating model must be approved by the internal sharia committee, the Central Bank and the Higher Shari'ah Authority, and published on the company's website, and that a new agency agreement regime governs how the company manages the fund's insurance and investment activities. If no board of trustees is appointed for the fund, an independent third party must sign the agency agreement on the fund's behalf.

Third, the regulation sets out what conventional insurers must do if they offer takaful through a window, which is a dedicated Islamic unit inside a conventional company. They must obtain Central Bank approval, establish a dedicated sharia governance framework, appoint an internal sharia supervision committee, designate a dedicated head for the business and keep separate accounts, including the fund, distinct from the insurance company's accounts. Al Tamimi explains that this reflects a change in the underlying law: Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, which took effect on September 16, 2025, allows conventional insurers to write takaful through an Islamic window without a separate dedicated takaful license. Previously, only a company licensed and incorporated as a takaful insurer could conduct takaful business, and conventional insurers were expressly barred from Islamic windows. The firm's assessment is that conventional insurers gain a lower-cost route into the takaful market and that existing takaful operators should expect more competition and review their fund charters, operating models and agency agreements against the new standards.

The Emirates 24|7 summary lists additional elements of the framework. It says takaful funds must have independent legal status, that each insurance type must have its own separate account, that any transfer of funds requires prior approval from the Central Bank, that solvency checks are enhanced, and that oversight of takaful windows is stronger. A photo caption says the Central Bank can subject a takaful fund to an independent solvency assessment. The captured page contained only this summary, so the detail behind those points was not available, and readers should consult the regulation itself for the exact text.

What is not known is also worth stating. Pinsent Masons reported no transition period or compliance deadline beyond the September 14 effective date, and the sources do not give capital figures, the number of firms affected or the cost of compliance. The articles do not say how many conventional insurers plan to open windows, and they do not describe the penalties for non-compliance. The commentary from Pinsent Masons lawyers describes the regulation as a significant step in modernising the UAE's takaful framework and says the fund requirement is intended to strengthen the segregation of policyholder funds, but these are expert views and not results.

This rule change sits alongside other developments in the UAE market. Earlier articles on this site covered the Central Bank's new insurance licensing rules, which make a firm's business plan central to its license. The takaful regulation is a separate instrument, aimed at one segment of the market, but it follows the same direction of travel: more explicit structure, clearer separation of customer money and tighter supervision.

For takaful participants, the practical effect should be a clearer legal structure around the money they contribute. For operators, the immediate tasks are to check whether their funds meet the legal-personality and segregation rules, to review whether their models comply with the wakala requirement, and, for conventional insurers with windows, to file for approval and set up separate accounts. For brokers and corporate buyers, the main point is that the market may soon have more suppliers of sharia-compliant cover, although the sources do not say when.
source_name: Pinsent Masons Out-Law (September 29, 2026), Al Tamimi & Company (August 11, 2026) and Emirates 24|7 (September 30, 2026)
image_alt: Financial documents and a calculator representing insurance regulation (illustrative)
key_points: The Central Bank of the UAE's 'Regulation regarding takaful insurance' took effect on September 14, 2026 and replaces the takaful rules introduced in 2022.

Every licensed takaful operator must set up a dedicated takaful insurance fund with its own legal personality, with assets and liabilities fully segregated from the company's, although claims remain enforceable against the company.
Operators must use a wakala-based model at all times, whereas earlier rules allowed wakala combined with mudaraba or another approved model, so firms using mudaraba may need to restructure.

Conventional insurers running takaful windows need Central Bank approval, a dedicated sharia governance framework, an internal sharia supervision committee, a dedicated head and separate accounts, and Emirates 24|7 reports that transfers of fund money need prior Central Bank approval.

Law firm commentary says the changes follow Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, which lets conventional insurers write takaful through Islamic windows without a separate license, and that the new rules give no transition period beyond the September 14 effective date.
why_it_matters: Takaful is Islamic insurance in which participants pool contributions, and the main regulatory question is how to keep participants' money separate from the operator's. The new rules tighten that separation while opening the market to conventional insurers, which could add competition but also raises compliance costs for firms that run takaful alongside conventional business.

title: Canada's Biggest Insurers Tell Ontario Brokers That AI Search Is Reshaping How Customers Shop: Intact Says 40% of Searches Now Use LLMs, While Definity Sees an Edge for Brokers
summary: At the Insurance Brokers Association of Ontario convention, executives from Intact, Definity, Wawanesa, Aviva and CAA Insurance said AI search tools are changing how customers research insurance; Intact put LLM share of searches at about 40%, Definity argued brokers benefit because models favor reviews and advice content, and the panel disagreed on how fast direct sales are growing.
description:
A panel of insurer executives at the 2026 convention of the Insurance Brokers Association of Ontario in Toronto produced a candid picture of how artificial intelligence is changing the way Canadians shop for insurance. Insurance Business Canada reported the discussion on October 27, 2026. The panel, moderated by IBAO chief executive Colin Simpson, brought together leaders from Definity, Intact, Wawanesa, Aviva and CAA Insurance. Their views differed on how quickly business is moving to direct channels, but they agreed that consumers increasingly start with AI tools, and that the old rules of search optimisation are being rewritten.

The most pointed argument came from Paul MacDonald, executive vice-president of personal insurance and digital channels at Definity. He said brokers hold an advantage as consumers use AI tools to research insurance. His reasoning is that traditional search engine optimisation rewards paid keywords, which insurers buy, while large language models, the technology behind chatbots such as ChatGPT, depend less on those signals. They look instead, he said, at reviews, blogs and information, which are the sort of content brokers have produced for years. He added that if you look at some LLM rankings, broker names come up very high. In the United States, he said, brokers are investing in web-facing AI faster than insurers are, and insurers are now building strategies for Reddit, Wikipedia and YouTube after years of blocking bots from their websites.

MacDonald offered practical advice to brokers: produce video, advice, referral content and customer feedback. He also noted a risk. AI tools draw heavily on Reddit posts, so customers sometimes arrive at brokerages with recommendations that are wrong for Ontario or for Canada. For direct writers, he said, the challenge is greater because they lack distribution and must have a stronger online presence. Definity launched the direct brand Sonnet, and he said the company used what it learned to build technology giving brokers similar real-time capabilities. His summary of consumer behaviour was that people research on their own but want a human when they buy.

Peter Janzen, executive vice-president and president of Intact Insurance Canada, put numbers on the change. He said that two or three years ago about 3 per cent of searches went through LLMs such as ChatGPT, and that today about 40 per cent do. These are his figures as reported, and the article does not cite a source for them. Intact, he said, sees the same trend in insurance. Janzen also gave a view of the market structure: a little over half of Canada's personal auto business is written direct, with a shift from brokers to direct of about a couple of basis points a year, while Intact writes about two-thirds of its business through brokers. Customers can get an online quote from Intact, and the company then passes the lead to a broker. It has also given brokers access to its commercial underwriting tool. His message to brokers was that customers want ease, a digital experience and, above all, value, and that brokers should build a niche around the value they add.

Evan Johnston, president and chief executive of Wawanesa, addressed a controversy. Earlier this year Wawanesa announced that it would explore a direct-to-consumer model, and the plan drew criticism. Johnston defended it while stating, in the article's words, that he 100 per cent believes the right way to buy insurance is through an independent broker. He said more personal lines, and possibly some small commercial business, could be sold direct in the future, and that Wawanesa is planning five to ten years ahead.

Paul Fletcher, managing director of Aviva Business and Broker Distribution, offered a smaller figure. Aviva's direct book is about 2 to 3 per cent of its personal lines business, and the company uses it selectively to stay close to consumer behaviour. He said the shift toward direct is real but that most customers are still served by brokers, and predicted that the channel mix will move back and forth over time.

The most sceptical voice was Matthew Turack, group president and chief operating officer of CAA Insurance. He said CAA sold only direct from 1974 until it opened to broker partners in 2016, and that brokers now account for more than half of its portfolio even though industry statistics still label CAA as entirely direct. He questioned how big the move toward direct really is, noting that CAA offers the same product and price through both channels. In effect, he argued that published channel statistics may overstate the direct share.

How should readers weigh these statements? They are opinions from executives with commercial interests, delivered to an audience of brokers. The 40 per cent figure for LLM share of searches is not documented, and the claim that LLMs favour broker content is an observation about some rankings, not a measured outcome across the market. What is verifiable from the report is the range of positions. Definity and Intact see AI search as a major change, and Definity thinks brokers are better placed to benefit. Wawanesa wants to explore direct but still praises the broker model, Aviva's direct share is small, and CAA argues that the direct share is smaller than it looks.

For brokers, the conclusion drawn by the panel is to invest in content that AI tools can find and cite, such as reviews, advice articles and videos, and to keep a human advantage at the point of purchase. For insurers, the message is that digital visibility now matters across multiple platforms, not just paid search. For customers, the risk noted in the article is practical: advice taken from a chatbot or a forum may not apply in their province, so checking with a licensed broker or insurer remains sensible. The channel shift, if it continues at a couple of basis points a year, is gradual, which gives both sides time to adapt.
image_alt: Laptop and documents representing online insurance shopping (illustrative)
key_points: Definity's Paul MacDonald said large language models favor the reviews, blogs and advice that brokers already produce over the paid keywords that insurers buy, so broker names rank high in some LLM results.
Intact Insurance Canada's Peter Janzen said about 3% of searches went through LLMs such as ChatGPT two or three years ago and about 40% do now, and that Intact sees the same trend in insurance.

A little over half of Canada's personal auto business is written direct, with a shift of about a couple of basis points a year from brokers to direct, while Intact writes about two-thirds of its business through brokers.

Wawanesa's Evan Johnston defended its plan to explore a direct model while saying the right way to buy is through an independent broker, and Aviva's direct book is only about 2% to 3% of personal lines.

CAA Insurance's Matthew Turack said brokers now account for more than half of CAA's portfolio even though industry statistics label it entirely direct, and questioned the scale of the shift to direct.
why_it_matters: Most Canadian personal insurance is still sold through brokers, so changes in how people research cover affect where premium is distributed. If AI tools send shoppers to the content brokers produce, the broker channel may gain visibility, but insurers are building their own strategies, and the sources are executive opinions rather than measured results.

title: Australian Insurers Spend Up to A$3.5 Billion a Year on Regulatory Compliance, and APRA Now Promises a 'Net Neutral' Burden: What Is Changing From 2027
summary: The Insurance Council of Australia puts annual regulatory compliance costs at A$2.5 billion to A$3.5 billion, 4% to 6% of gross written premium, and APRA said on September 24, 2026 that its 2026-27 measures aim for a broadly net neutral burden, with new reinsurance standards starting January 1, 2027.
description:
How much does it cost to comply with insurance regulation in Australia, and who pays? The industry's answer is up to A$3.5 billion a year, and the prudential regulator's answer is that it is trying to keep its own contribution to that bill from rising. Insurance Business Australia reported on September 25, 2026 that the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority had set out a position on the regulatory burden in an article published the previous day, as the Insurance Council of Australia (ICA) continued to press for what it calls better regulation, not less.

The industry's figure comes from the ICA's Cost of Regulatory Burden report, published in November 2025. It estimated that Australian general insurers spend between A$2.5 billion and A$3.5 billion a year on regulatory compliance, which is equal to 4 to 6 per cent of gross written premium. The report counted more than 30,000 obligations, enforced by 25 authorities across 300 regulatory instruments. In a November 2025 letter to the Council of Financial Regulators, the ICA said its goal was not less regulation but better regulation: rules that safeguard customers without unnecessary complexity or cost. ICA chief executive Andrew Hall described an October 2025 roundtable with APRA, ASIC and industry leaders as a timely and important conversation. Richard Klipin, chief executive of the National Insurance Brokers Association, was quoted from the Drova Insurance Outlook Report 2026, saying that in reality it is one plus one plus one plus one, and over many years you layer on lots of regulation.

A worked example in the ICA report shows how overlap arises. After a cyber incident, an insurer must notify APRA within 72 hours and ASIC within 30 days, and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner on a separate timeline, with each regulator using different definitions and documentation requirements. The point is not that any one notification is unreasonable, but that the same event triggers several processes that do not align.

APRA's response came on September 24, 2026, in an APRA Explains article under its Getting the balance right strategic agenda. The regulator said its 2026-27 measures were designed to offset the burden of new requirements, aiming for a broadly net neutral regulatory impact. In July 2026, APRA had published a Statement of Intent in reply to the Commonwealth Government's Statement of Expectations, in which it committed to streamline information requests, simplify processes, address duplication and publish key performance indicators on reducing burden. APRA also reported that it had shared 30 per cent more data with external stakeholders over the previous 12 months, which it said reduced duplicate requests. Member Suzanne Smith said reducing unnecessary burden does not mean lowering standards.

Alongside the burden agenda, APRA has finalised concrete changes. On July 7, 2026, it finalised amendments to the general insurance reinsurance framework, with the standards taking effect on January 1, 2027. The Appointed Actuary's role expands to determine the capital treatment of certain reinsurance arrangements, which reduces the number of cases that must be referred to APRA. Smith said the amendments modernise the prudential framework and give insurers greater flexibility to access reinsurance arrangements. The article says the review began during a period of significant reinsurance market pressure, and cites EBM Insurance and Risk's May 2026 market report as saying conditions have since eased and that the commercial market stayed soft through the first half of 2026. An earlier article on this site covered the reinsurance standards in more detail.

In life insurance, APRA finalised reduced capital requirements for annuity products, intended to bring Australian settings closer to those of other jurisdictions. APRA says the changes are not expected to transform the annuity market but should support more competitive pricing without increasing policyholder risk. The article places this in the context of a superannuation system of about A$4.1 trillion in assets as of March 2025, according to the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia.

What comes next is a broader policy simplification package and continuing reforms under the Financial Accountability Regime. APRA's promise of a net neutral impact is a useful commitment, but the sources do not describe how it will be measured, so the test will be the key performance indicators that APRA says it will publish. It is also worth noting that APRA is only one of the 25 authorities in the ICA's count. Even a regulator that succeeds in simplifying its own requests cannot, alone, reduce obligations imposed by ASIC, the privacy regulator, state governments and others.

Why does this matter beyond the industry? Compliance costs are a component of the expense ratio of every insurer, and expense ratios feed into premiums. If the ICA's estimate of 4 to 6 per cent of gross written premium is right, then a significant share of what a household pays for home or motor insurance covers the cost of meeting regulatory requirements. That does not mean regulation is unnecessary, since much of it exists to protect consumers, and the ICA itself argues for better rules and not fewer. But it does mean that simplification, if achieved, could eventually reduce costs for policyholders.

For insurers, the immediate tasks are practical: prepare for the reinsurance standards that start on January 1, 2027, understand the larger role of the Appointed Actuary, and watch for APRA's published burden indicators and simplification package. For customers, the signal is that the regulator and industry now agree on the problem, even if they may not agree on the size of the solution.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia (September 25, 2026), citing the Insurance Council of Australia and APRA
image_alt: Documents and a laptop representing regulatory compliance work (illustrative)
key_points: The Insurance Council of Australia's November 2025 report estimated compliance costs of A$2.5 billion to A$3.5 billion a year, equal to 4% to 6% of gross written premium.
More than 30,000 obligations, enforced by 25 authorities across 300 regulatory instruments, underpin that cost.

On September 24, 2026 APRA said its 2026-27 measures are designed to offset the burden of new requirements, aiming for a broadly net neutral impact, and in July it committed to streamlining information requests and publishing burden-reduction indicators.

APRA finalised changes to the general insurance reinsurance framework on July 7, 2026, effective January 1, 2027, giving the Appointed Actuary a bigger role in the capital treatment of certain reinsurance and reducing referrals to APRA.

After a cyber incident an insurer must notify APRA within 72 hours, ASIC within 30 days and the privacy regulator on another timeline, each with different definitions, which the ICA cites as an example of overlap.
why_it_matters: Compliance cost is built into premiums, so the burden the ICA describes is ultimately paid by customers. A commitment to keep new rules net neutral is a promise, not a result, and the figures to watch are APRA's burden indicators and how the 2027 reinsurance standards work in practice.

title: IRDAI Is Enforcing Insurers' Expense Limits: Four Companies Barred From Opening Branches for Six Months, 23 Breached in FY25, and a Distribution Overhaul Is Open for Comment Until October 31
summary: IRDAI barred Edelweiss Life, Pramerica Life, ACKO General and Niva Bupa Health from opening new places of business for six months over FY25 expense-of-management breaches, with 23 insurers exceeding limits, while its consultation on distribution costs drew more than 650 submissions and had its deadline extended to October 31, 2026.
description:
India's insurance regulator has begun using restrictions on growth to enforce limits on how much insurers can spend. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) barred four insurers from opening new places of business for six months because they breached expense of management limits in the financial year 2024-25, according to reports in August 2026. The move comes while the regulator is consulting on a broader reform of distribution costs, a consultation that drew more than 650 submissions and whose deadline was extended on October 26.

The facts of the August action are as follows. Outlook Money reported on August 25, 2026 that IRDAI had barred Edelweiss Life Insurance, Pramerica Life Insurance, ACKO General Insurance and Niva Bupa Health Insurance from opening new places of business for six months. Free Press Journal, carrying an IANS report on August 20, described the order against Niva Bupa in more detail. IRDAI issued it on August 19, 2026, a day before the company announced it, directing the company not to open a new place of business for six months from the date of the order. The reason was that Niva Bupa breached prescribed limits on expenses of management in FY 2024-25 and was warned for not complying. IRDAI had sought an explanation, and the company made submissions in response. The company, which is backed by the UK-based healthcare group Bupa, said it complied with the limits for FY 2025-26 and for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, and is on track for FY 2026-27. It cited the IRDAI (Expenses of Management, including Commission of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, said it is evaluating the order, and its shares closed 1.3 per cent lower after the announcement. An industry official told Outlook Money that the FY25 cases went through reviews and hearings before restrictions were imposed.

Expenses of management, abbreviated EoM, cover the costs of running and distributing an insurer's business, including commissions paid to distributors and intermediaries, staff, technology and day-to-day operations. Outlook Money explains that IRDAI lets insurers vary individual expense heads, but total expenses must remain within a prescribed ceiling. It cites limits of 30 per cent of gross written premium for general insurers and up to 35 per cent for standalone health insurers, and says life insurers have separate limits that depend on product type, without giving those figures. IRDAI's FY25 annual report showed that 23 insurers, eight life and 15 non-life, exceeded their limits and sought regulatory forbearance. Experts quoted expect similar action against companies still outside the permitted range, though they say the restriction is unlikely to have a large near-term effect on the four insurers, since they already have established distribution networks. Pressure is likely to be greater on insurers that depend heavily on commissions and intermediated sales, because commission costs can swing sharply from year to year. The article's key takeaway is that expense limits are no longer just a reporting requirement.

A separate summary dated October 7, 2026 by BimaBazaar lists further items, and because it is a single source and the sources reviewed here did not corroborate every point, they should be treated cautiously. It reports that ACKO General was restricted in a separate order and that Niva Bupa was directed not to add branches from August 19. It also reports a Rs 1 crore penalty on ICICI Lombard General Insurance under Section 102 of the Insurance Act, 1938, following an onsite inspection in September 2019, for lapses in outsourcing, vendor management, internal controls and governance, along with advisories on unallocated premium and delays in freelook cancellation requests. It adds a warning about a fake grievance website that IRDAI says is not an official platform, and a proposed Public Insurance Registry consultation under the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025, which would connect insurers, intermediaries, reinsurers, financial institutions, government agencies and policyholders on a consent basis.

The enforcement matters more because of the policy debate under way. IRDAI's consultation paper, Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution, proposes lower expense of management limits and product-level commission caps. Sahi reported on October 26, 2026 that IRDAI extended the deadline for comments from October 25 to October 31 after more than 650 stakeholder submissions. Respondents raised concerns about distribution architecture, revenue implications and agent earnings, with insurers and agents focusing on commission caps, expense limits and the effect on distribution revenue. IRDAI proposed capping credit life commission paid to lenders at 2 per cent for single-premium policies and 2.5 per cent for multi-year policies. HDFC Life and other life insurers have defended credit life policies in discussions, the Reserve Bank of India said it would submit comments on the impact on banks' fee income, and intermediaries and agent federations have pushed for higher commission tiers to offset rising operating costs. The Sahi page notes that its content may include AI-assisted material, so these points should be verified against IRDAI's own publications.

Taken together, the two threads show a regulator tightening control of costs from two directions. The first is enforcement of existing limits, using a restriction that goes to the heart of an insurer's growth plans: the ability to open branches. The second is proposed reform that would reset the limits and commission structure. The sources do not say when final guidelines will be issued; the Sahi page suggests they could follow the October 31 deadline, but that is its commentary, not an announcement.

For customers, expense limits matter because a smaller share of premium spent on distribution leaves more for claims and reserves, although lower commissions can also reduce the incentive for advisers to sell. For insurers, the message is to manage expenses within the limits each year, since breaches can lead to sanctions even when later years are compliant. For banks and agents, the consultation signals that commission income may change. The next items to watch are IRDAI's decisions after the consultation closes, any further orders for FY25 breaches, and how insurers describe distribution costs in their second-quarter results.
source_name: Free Press Journal/IANS (August 20, 2026), Outlook Money (August 25, 2026) and Sahi (October 26, 2026)
image_alt: Calculator and financial papers representing insurer expenses (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI barred Edelweiss Life, Pramerica Life, ACKO General and Niva Bupa Health from opening new places of business for six months over breaches of expense of management limits in FY 2024-25.
Niva Bupa's order is dated August 19, 2026 and says it complied in FY26 and the quarter to June 30, 2026, while shares closed 1.3% lower after the announcement.

IRDAI's FY25 annual report showed 23 insurers, 8 life and 15 non-life, exceeded expense limits and sought forbearance; the limits cited are 30% of gross written premium for general insurers and up to 35% for standalone health insurers.

IRDAI's 'Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution' consultation drew more than 650 submissions, and the deadline moved from October 25 to October 31, 2026, with credit life commission proposed at 2% for single-premium and 2.5% for multi-year policies.

A single-source October 7 summary also reports a Rs 1 crore penalty on ICICI Lombard over outsourcing and governance lapses and a consultation on a Public Insurance Registry, details not independently checked here.
why_it_matters: Expense limits stop insurers from spending too much of premium on running and selling policies, and the orders show they are now backed by real restrictions. Combined with the proposed distribution cost reforms, they point to tighter control of commissions and branch growth, which would affect agents, banks and customers.
